extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, forensic investigators, judges, and legal professionals assessing witness testimony
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating female testimony in criminal cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forensic practitioners and judges on how to interpret, evaluate, and investigate testimony and behavior of women and girls, with emphasis on sex-specific psychological and physiological influences (e.g., menstruation, reproductive role, imagination/productivity differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat circumlocutive expressions and rounded figures cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumlocutive expressions (e.g., 'half-a-dozen' or four syllables instead of 'six', or mnemonic phrases like 'the bell in the dome at St. Stephen's has as many nicks as the year has days') are often chosen to make an assertion general or as mnemonic aids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: such statements may simply 'round out' figures or require testing for reliability; do not accept them at face value without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering unintelligible foreign words by loud repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words are often changed into senseless words of similar sound when heard by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When unintelligible words are heard, very loud repeated restatement of the word will help in finding the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate women's testimony by male standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Men and women have different somatic and psychic natures; men cannot wholly put themselves in a woman's place, so applying male standards to female testimony leads to systematic mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize sex-differences and avoid uncritical application of male norms when valuing women's statements or deeds; seek to study the manifestations of the 'eternal feminine' rather than assume equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use popular maxims and common usage as a corrective average (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular conceptions, proverbs, and legal usage embody an 'average' distilled from many experiences and may be less misleading than single observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such maxims as providing a kind of average guide that can reduce extreme error; nevertheless, be aware averages are imperfect and use them cautiously—not as absolute truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer scientific disciplines over poetry/memoirs for forensic judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic and literary descriptions of women often do not mirror real life and may mislead the criminalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on anatomy, physiology, anthropology, universal history, and serious specialized literature rather than poets or memoirists when forming forensic judgments about women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider women's biological and culturally formed psychical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond physiological traits (menstruation, pregnancy, childbirth, suckling, climacterium), psychical conditions shaped by civilization and custom (e.g., enforced secrecy, indirect expression) substantially influence women's behavior and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study both somatic and psychical conditions together to explain conduct and statements; these influences can be decisive in interpreting testimony or motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heusinger productive vs. reproductive imagination heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Women tend to have 'reproductive' imaginative power (reworking existing forms), while men tend to show more 'productive' originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criminal plans and in fabricated testimony, an independently worked-out, original plan or invented narrative suggests masculine (productive) origins; imitative, derivative, or 'reproductive' plans/narratives suggest feminine origin. Use this only as a cautionary heuristic to raise suspicion, not as direct evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use productive vs. reproductive features of testimony to detect invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When part of a testimony seems incorrect or invented, distinguishing whether the invention is 'productive' (original, elaborate) or 'reproductive' (imitative, derivative) may help identify the source and truthfulness, especially given typical gendered tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a suspected lie appears in 'tragic' or highly elaborate (productive) form and the witness is a man, or in 'sonnet'/'reproductive' form and the witness is a woman, increase suspicion. This method is not evidential by itself but may justify further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always assess whether sex-specific states (e.g., menstruation) were present at time of event or testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Menstruation can significantly alter perception, emotion, and the content or truthfulness of testimony—especially at menarche or during active menses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine if the event was perceived or the testimony given during menses; if so, be alert to exaggeration or invention. Where necessary, obtain a medical examination and the court physician's report about onset and diseased conditions, and then interpret that medically informed report psychologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require court physician input on menstruation-related questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must understand the influence of menstruation and should require the court physician to report when menstruation began and whether diseased conditions were apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge interprets the physician’s factual report in psychological terms; do not rely solely on lay impressions or casual signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize typical menstrual timing and its psychological effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Menstruation normally begins around 13–15 years, ends around 45–50 years, typically recurs every ~27–28 days and lasts 3–5 days; sexual impulse is often intensified after menses and mental life can show significant alterations during menses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these general timings when considering the plausibility of menstrual influence, but verify individual variation via medical evidence rather than stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on popular physical signs of menstruation; prefer direct inquiry/examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly credited external signs (significant shining of eyes, bad breath, particular appearance) are unreliable indicators of menstruation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct questioning and physician examination to determine menstrual state; treat popular signs as weak cues at best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be especially cautious with testimony from newly menstruating girls
rubrics_metrics.description: At the onset of puberty (menarche) girls may be unusually tender, spiritual, and prone to romantic or extraordinary fantasies leading to false accusations (e.g., seduction, rape, arson, slander).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where allegations come from girls at menarche, check dates relative to menses, seek corroboration, obtain testimony about prior trustworthiness, and consider medical examination; these unreliable tendencies often subside once menstrual cycles stabilize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate menstrual-influenced testimony via acquaintance reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct questions about menstruation are often answered falsely by the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask persons who know the woman or girl well about her trustworthiness and behavior before menarche or before the suspected menstrual-influenced episode; use such third-party testimony to strengthen or weaken the suspicion of menstrual influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing of proceedings relative to menstrual cycle when accusations are menstrual-linked
rubrics_metrics.description: Many complaints by menstruating women fall through; cyclical emotionality can influence both accusations and their persistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that conducting trial stages at arbitrary points in the month may capture similar emotional states; timing alone does not resolve truth, but awareness of cycle effects can inform scheduling and re-examination strategies (e.g., re-examine four weeks later if warranted).
